terms: adjugate; classical adjoint; cofactor matrix; adjugate inverse formula; determinant crite- rion for invertibility.

For invertible n × n matrices, det(adj A) = (det A) . The identity extends to singular matrices
for n ≥ 2. If rank is at most n − 2, every (n − 1)-minor vanishes and the adjugate is zero. If rank
is n − 1, the adjugate is nonzero but its columns lie in the one-dimensional kernel, so it has rank
one. Classical adjoint here is distinct from conjugate transpose.

question.text:
A 4 × 4 real matrix has rank 2. What is adj A?
(A) I (B) A (C) 0 (D) A matrix of rank one (E) A matrix of rank two
4

solution.text:
Each cofactor is a signed 3 × 3 minor. Every such minor is zero because the full matrix has
rank only 2. Thus all adjugate entries vanish.

question.text:
If an n × n matrix, n ≥ 2, has rank n − 1, what is the rank of its adjugate?
(A) It cannot be determined
(B) 1
(C) n − 1
(D) n
(E) 0

solution.text:
At least one (n − 1)-minor is nonzero, so the adjugate is nonzero. Since A adj A = 0, its
columns lie in the one-dimensional kernel of A, forcing rank one.
